3.text: provisions. For a woman, the spear and the bow are omitted, but there are

4.text: added scraper and work-bag with needle-case and thimble.

5.text: Among other taboos connected with the funeral must be mentioned the

6.text: interdiction against beating the drum for three nights during the time of the

7.text: ceremony. The day on which the remains are carried away to the funeral

8.text: place is especially dangerous. The beating of the drum might call the

9.text: deceased back to the house. In corroboration of this idea I was told several

10.text: stories, in which a shamanistic performance brought a deceased person back

11.text: to the house, and the corpse dropped through the roof to its former place.

12.text: Then the ceremonial, with all the incantations, had to be repeated, again.

13.text: Another prescription forbids any kind of woman’s work with needle and

14.text: scraper, during the same period of time as in the first case, and especially

15.text: in the evening. Both rules refer to all houses of the camp or the village,

16.text: and even to all other settlements in the vicinity.

17.text: Dressing of the Dead Body. — Among the reindeer-breeders, two

18.text: reindeer are slaughtered in the morning, and a small fire is made before the

19.text: entrance of the tent, which receives the usual sacrifice. Then two, three, or

20.text: four couples of nearest relatives of the deceased, men and woman in equal

21.text: number, enter the inner room and proceed to dress the body for the funeral.

22.text: They are called “followers.” Ameal is spread upon the skin covering the
22.note: Printed as one word 'Ameal' (for 'A meal') — printer's error, keyed as printed per §2.14.

23.text: body. The part of the skin close to the mouth of the departed one is

24.text: ripped, and crumbs of meat and tallow are thrust in under, in order that he

25.text: may have his part of the food. Then the “followers” take off their shoes and

26.text: stockings, and turn up their pantaloons as high as possible. They sit down

27.text: on both sides of the body, and thrust their bare legs under the corpse, so

28.text: that it is entirely lifted from the lower skin, and rests on the legs of the

29.text: “followers.” After that, they proceed to bid the last farewell to the deceased.

30.text: This is begun by the husband or wife, the father or mother, and is then

31.text: repeated by every one of the “followers.”

32.text: For this, the acting party takes one of the hands of the deceased, and

33.text: chafes with it his bare waist and buttocks. After that, the party touches in

34.text: the same manner the buttocks of the deceased, repeating words of improvised

35.text: farewell. For instance, a husband said in my hearing, to his deceased wife,

36.text: “Well, well! What can I do? We have lived together for so many years,

37.text: and now you are going away! Do not keep an evil mind against me! My

38.text: head was never very strong. If I acted unfairly towards you, have no bad
